{{Short description|Identity in analytic number theory}}
In mathematics and [[analytic number theory]], '''Vaughan's identity''' is an [[Identity (mathematics)|identity]] found by {{harvs|txt=yes|authorlink=Robert Charles Vaughan (mathematician)|last=Vaughan|first=R. C. |year=1977}} that can be used to simplify  [[I.M. Vinogradov|Vinogradov]]'s [[Vinogradov's theorem|work]] on [[trigonometric sum]]s. It can be used to estimate summatory functions of the form
:<math>\sum_{n \leq N} f(n)\Lambda(n)</math>
where ''f'' is some [[arithmetic function]] of the natural integers ''n'', whose values in applications are often roots of unity, and Λ is the [[von Mangoldt function]].

==Procedure for applying the method==

The motivation for Vaughan's construction of his identity is briefly discussed at the beginning of Chapter 24 in Davenport. For now, we will skip over most of the technical details motivating the identity and its usage in applications, and instead focus on the setup of its construction by parts. Following from the reference, we construct four distinct sums based on the expansion of the [[logarithmic derivative]] of the [[Riemann zeta function]] in terms of functions which are partial [[Dirichlet series]] respectively truncated at the upper bounds of <math>U</math> and <math>V</math>, respectively. More precisely, we define <math>F(s) = \sum_{m \leq U} \Lambda(m) m^{-s}</math> and <math>G(s) = \sum_{d \leq V} \mu(d) d^{-s}</math>, which leads us to the exact identity that

:<math>-\frac{\zeta^{\prime}(s)}{\zeta(s)} = F(s) - \zeta(s) F(s) G(s) - \zeta^{\prime}(s) G(s) + \left(-\frac{\zeta^{\prime}(s)}{\zeta(s)} - F(s)\right) (1-\zeta(s) G(s)). </math>

This last expansion implies that we can write

:<math>\Lambda(n) = a_1(n) + a_2(n) + a_3(n) + a_4(n), </math>

where the component functions are defined to be

:<math>\begin{align} 
a_1(n) & := \Biggl\{\begin{matrix} \Lambda(n), & \text{ if } n \leq U; \\ 0, & \text{ if } n > U\end{matrix} \\ 
a_2(n) & := - \sum_{\stackrel{mdr = n}{\stackrel{m \leq U}{d \leq V}}} \Lambda(m) \mu(d) \\ 
a_3(n) & := \sum_{\stackrel{hd=n}{d \leq V}} \mu(d) \log(h) \\ 
a_4(n) & := -\sum_{\stackrel{mk=n}{\stackrel{m > U}{k > 1}}} \Lambda(m) \left(\sum_{\stackrel{d|k}{d \leq V}} \mu(d)\right). 
\end{align} 
</math>

We then define the corresponding summatory functions for <math>1 \leq i \leq 4</math> to be

:<math>S_i(N) := \sum_{n \leq N} f(n) a_i(n), </math>

so that we can write

:<math>\sum_{n \leq N} f(n) \Lambda(n) = S_1(N) + S_2(N) + S_3(N) + S_4(N). </math>

Finally, at the conclusion of a multi-page argument of technical and at times delicate estimations of these sums,<ref>N.b., which if you read Davenport frequently enough will lead you to conclude evident properties about the difficulty level of the complete details to proving Vaughan's identity carefully.</ref> we obtain the following form of '''Vaughan's identity''' when we assume that <math>|f(n)| \leq 1,\ \forall n</math>, <math>U,V \geq 2</math>, and <math>UV \leq N</math>:

:<math>\sum_{n \leq N} f(n) \Lambda(n) \ll U + (\log N) \times \sum_{t\leq UV}\left(\max_{w} \left|\sum_{w \leq r \leq \frac{N}{t}} f(rt)\right|\right) + 
       \sqrt{N} (\log N)^3 \times \max_{U \leq M \leq N/V} \max_{V \leq j \leq N/M}\left(\sum_{V < k \leq N/M} \left| 
       \sum_{\stackrel{M < m \leq 2M}{\stackrel{m \leq N/k}{m \leq N/j}}} f(mj) \bar{f(mk)}\right|\right)^{1/2} \mathbf{(V1)}.</math>

It is remarked that in some instances sharper estimates can be obtained from Vaughan's identity by treating the component sum <math>S_2</math> more carefully by expanding it in the form of

:<math>S_2 = \sum_{t \leq UV} \longmapsto \sum_{t \leq U} + \sum_{U < t \leq UV} =: S_2^{\prime} + S_2^{\prime\prime}. </math>

The optimality of the upper bound obtained by applying Vaughan's identity appears to be application-dependent with respect to the best functions <math>U = f_U(N)</math> and <math>V = f_V(N)</math> we can choose to input into equation (V1). See the applications cited in the next section for specific examples that arise in the different contexts respectively considered by multiple authors.

==Applications==

* Vaughan's identity has been used to simplify the proof of the [[Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem]] and to study [[Kummer sum]]s (see the references and external links below).
* In Chapter 25 of Davenport, one application of Vaughan's identity is to estimate an important prime-related [[exponential sum]] of [[Vinogradov]] defined by

:<math>S(\alpha) := \sum_{n \leq N} \Lambda(n) e\left(n\alpha\right).</math>

In particular, we obtain an asymptotic upper bound for these sums (typically evaluated at [[irrational]] <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}</math>) whose rational approximations satisfy

:<math>\left| \alpha - \frac{a}{q} \right| \leq \frac{1}{q^2}, (a, q) = 1, </math>

of the form

:<math>S(\alpha) \ll \left(\frac{N}{\sqrt{q}} + N^{4/5} + \sqrt{Nq}\right) (\log N)^4. </math>

The argument for this estimate follows from Vaughan's identity by proving by a somewhat intricate argument that

:<math>S(\alpha) \ll \left(UV + q + \frac{N}{\sqrt{U}} + \frac{N}{\sqrt{V}} + \frac{N}{\sqrt{q}} + \sqrt{Nq}\right) (\log(qN))^4, </math>

and then deducing the first formula above in the non-trivial cases when <math>q \leq N</math> and with <math>U = V = N^{2/5}</math>.

* Another application of Vaughan's identity is found in Chapter 26 of Davenport where the method is employed to derive estimates for sums ([[exponential sum]]s) of [[primes|three primes]].
* Examples of Vaughan's identity in practice are given as the following references / citations in [https://mathoverflow.net/questions/55274/other-applications-of-vaughans-lemma  this informative post]:.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Tao|first1=T.|title=Every integer greater than 1 is the sum of at most five primes|year=2012|class=math.NT|eprint=1201.6656}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Conrey|first1=J. B.|title=More than two fifths of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are on the critical line|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|date=1989|volume=399|pages=1–26}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan|title=On the distribution of square-free numbers|journal=Recent Progress in Analytic Number Theory, H. Halberstam (Ed.), C. Hooley (Ed.)|date=1981|volume=1|pages=247–256}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=D. R. Heath-Brown and S. J. Patterson|title=The distribution of Kummer sums at prime arguments|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|date=1979|volume=310|pages=110–130}}</ref>

==Generalizations==

Vaughan's identity was generalized by {{harvtxt|Heath-Brown|1982}}.
